{{Short description|Statistical field}}

'''Bayes space''' is a [[function space]] defined as an [[equivalence class]] of measures with the same [[Null set|null-sets]]. Two measures are defined to be equivalent if they are proportional. The basic ideas of Bayes spaces have their roots in [[Compositional data|Compositional Data Analysis]] and the Aitchison geometry.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Egozcue |first1=J. The basic structure of the Bayes space is that of a [[vector space]], with addition and multiplication being defined by perturbation and powering.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van den Boogart |first1=K. G. |last2 = Egozcue |first2= J. J. |last3=Pawlowsky-Glahn | first3= V. |date=2010 |title=Bayes linear spaces |url=https://www.raco.cat/index.php/SORT/article/view/217213 |journal=SORT: Statistics and Operations Research Transactions |volume=34 |pages=201–222}}</ref> The space is formed over a <math>\sigma</math>-finite reference/base measure, denoted <math>\lambda</math> or <math>P</math> depending on whether it is infinite or finite. Densities are considered as [[Radon–Nikodym theorem|Radon-Nikodym]] derivatives of the measures with same null-sets as the base measure, and are equivalent if they are proportional. In case of finite base measures, [[Hilbert space]] structure can be achieved by defining a [[Compositional data#Linear transformations|centered log-ratio transformation]] on the measures, mapping them to a subset of <math>L^2(P)</math> consisting of functions integrating to 0.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van den Boogart |first1=K. G. |last2 = Egozcue |first2= J. J. |last3=Pawlowsky-Glahn | first3= V. |date=2014 |title=Bayes Hilbert spaces |url= https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/anzs.12074 |journal=Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics | volume = 56 |issue=2 |pages=171–194 |doi=10.1111/anzs.12074 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
[[File:Visualisation of the clr-transformations.jpg|thumb|720x720px|Visualisation of clr-transfomrations of densities from [[Chi-squared distribution]] and [[Normal distribution]], with truncations to <math>(0,3)</math> and <math>(-2,5)</math> respectively.]]
For data analysis, density functions are typically estimated using so-called ZB-splines<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Machalová |first=Jitka |last2=Talská |first2=Renáta |last3=Hron |first3=Karel |last4=Gába |first4=Aleš |date=2021-06-01 |title=Compositional splines for representation of density functions |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00180-020-01042-7 |journal=Computational Statistics |language=en |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=1031–1064 |doi=10.1007/s00180-020-01042-7 |issn=1613-9658|arxiv=1905.06858 }}</ref> to smooth over a [[histogram]] of the data, using [[Kernel density estimation]], or using a combination of the two.

== Definitions and main results ==
Consider a finite base measure <math>P</math> (not necessarily a [[probability measure]]) on a domain <math>\Omega</math>. This may be a uniform distribution on a bounded interval, or it can be a Radon-Nikodym derivative of the Lebesgue measure (the [[Normal distribution|Gaussian distribution]], for example). In practice, <math>\Omega</math> is often truncated to a bounded interval. If we take two densities <math>f,g</math> with respect to <math>P</math>, they are said to be B-equivalent if there exists a <math>c>0</math> s.t <math>f(x)= c \cdot g(x)</math>, denoted <math>f=_B g</math> (the convention <math>c \cdot \infty = \infty</math> is used in cases where a measure is infinite). It can be shown that <math>(=_B)</math> is an equivalence relation. The Bayes space <math>B(P)</math> is defined as the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] of all measures with the same null-sets in <math>\Omega</math> as <math>P</math> under the equivalence relation <math>(=_B)</math>.

The first challenge to analysing density functions is that <math>B(P)</math> is not [[Vector space|linear space]] under ordinary addition and multiplication since the ordinary difference between two densities would not be non-negative everywhere. Like in the [[Compositional data|Aitchison geometry]] for finite dimensional data, perturbation and powering is defined for densities:

'''Perturbation'''

<math display="inline">(f\oplus g) (x)=_Bf(x)\cdot g(x)</math>

'''Powering'''

<math display="inline">\alpha \odot f(x)=_B f(x)^\alpha</math>

where <math>f(x),\text{ }g(x)</math> are densities in <math>B(P)</math> and <math>\alpha</math> is some [[real number]]. It can be shown using the properties of multiplication and powering of real numbers that <math>(B(P),\oplus,\odot)</math> forms a vector space over the real numbers.

The definition of Bayes space does not strictly require a finite reference measure <math>P</math>. If Bayes space is defined over an infinite reference measure <math>\lambda</math>, it must be <math>\sigma</math>-finite (like the [[Lebesgue measure]]). The finite reference measure is, however, necessary for adding Hilbert space structure to a subset of <math>B(P)</math>. Consider the subspace

<math display="inline">B^p(P)=\{f\in B(P)|\int_\Omega |\log(f(x))|^p dP(x)<\infty\}</math>. For <math>p=2</math>, this is a [[linear subspace]] and isometrically isomorphic to the Hilbert space <math display="inline">L_0^2(P)=\{g\in L^2(P):\int_\Omega g(x) dP(x)=0\}</math> via the centered log-ratio (clr) transformation <math>\text{clr}(f(x))=\log(f(x))-\frac{1}{P(\Omega)}\int \log(f(x)) dP(x)\in L_0^2(P)</math>. The subspace of log-square integrable functions is termed the Bayes Hilbert space. It can be shown that the clr transformation is a linear isomorphism between the two spaces. Defining an [[Inner product space|inner product]] on <math>B^2(P)</math> as the inner product of the clr transformations will provide the Hilbert space structure for <math>B^2(P)</math>, obtaining the centered log-ratio transformation as a linear isometry. Specifically,  this results in the Aitchison distance between two densities in the same Bayes Hilbert space

<math>d(f,g)=\int (\text{clr}(f(x)-\text{clr}(g(x))^2dP(x)</math>

which for densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure on an interval <math>\Omega=[a,b]</math> "simplifies" to <math>d(f,g)=\int_a^b \left(\left[\text{log}(f(x)-\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b \text{log}(f(x)) dx\right]-\left[\text{log}(g(x)-\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b \text{log}(g(x)) dx\right]\right)^2dx</math>.

== Multivariate densities ==
The measure <math>P</math> does not have to be univariate (one-dimensional), but can also be defined as a [[product measure]] on [[Cartesian product]]s, characterising bivariate (two-dimensional) or multivariate densities. The geometric structure of Hilbert spaces can be used to decompose multivariate densities orthogonally into independent and interaction parts using the concept of "geometric marginals".<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Hron |first1=K. |last2=Machalová |first2= J. |last3=Menafoglio |first3=A. |title=Bivariate densities in Bayes spaces: orthogonal decomposition and spline representation |journal= Statistical Papers|date=2023 |volume=64 |issue=5 |pages=1629–1667 |doi=10.1007/s00362-022-01359-z |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00362-022-01359-z|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":GHN23">{{Cite journal |last1=Genest |first1=C. |last2=Hron |first2= K. |last3=Nešlehová |first3=J. G. |title=Orthogonal decomposition of multivariate densities in Bayes spaces and relation with their copula-based representation |journal= Journal of Multivariate Analysis|date=2023 |volume=198 |issue=5 |article-number=105228 |doi=10.1016/j.jmva.2023.105228 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite arXiv |last1=Škorňa |first1=S. |last2=Machalová |first2= J.|last3=Burkotová |first3=J. |last4=Hron |first4= K. |last5=Greven |first5=S. |title=Approximation of bivariate densities with compositional splines |date=2024 |class=stat.ME |eprint=2405.11615}}</ref> This decomposition has relations to [[Copula (statistics)|copula theory]].<ref name=":GHN23" /> The geometry in <math>B^2(P)</math> defines norms on densities that can be used to quantify "relative simplicial deviance", which is measure of how much of a bivariate distribution can be explained by the interaction part;<ref name=":0" /> in the multivariate case the relative simplicial deviance can be generalised to the "information composition".<ref name=":GHN23" />
